name: Seaborgium

discovery.discoverer: Contested — claims by teams at Dubna, USSR and Berkeley, USA

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced only via particle accelerator fusion, atom by atom.
majorUses: No practical applications — pure superheavy-element research
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive; produced and studied only as individual atoms with half-lives of seconds to minutes.
notableCharacteristics: Named directly after Glenn T. Seaborg, the chemist behind the discovery of ten transuranium elements — making it one of the very few elements named after a scientist who was still alive at the time.
ncertRelevance: named after a living scientist (rare exception)
whyHere: Predicted to sit in Group 6 alongside tungsten and molybdenum, seaborgium's expected preference for a +6 oxidation state follows the same trend down that group, a prediction later single-atom chemistry experiments have broadly supported.
didYouKnow: Seaborgium is one of the only elements ever named after a person who was still living at the time — Glenn Seaborg was reportedly delighted, joking that he could now tell his grandchildren to look him up in the periodic table.
genZNote: Named after a scientist who was literally still alive to see it happen. Certified 'flowers while you can still smell them' moment.
